questions.question: Wave 00's biggest gate. Database tests can't currently prove anything: the owner role bypasses RLS (a fresh tenant still sees three weeks of dev rows) and the app role can't INSERT INTO tenants to seed. 100+ tasks in bands A/C/D/E/H are written against whichever contract you pick, and changing it later invalidates them. (psot-00-01)

options.label: Two roles: seed as owner, assert as app (Recommended)
options.description: Seed and tear down through the owner DSN; run every assertion through the RLS-enforcing app role. Tests then exercise the same policy path production does, so a missing or wrong RLS policy FAILS the test. Costs a slightly more complex fixture.

options.label: One DSN + tenant_id filter per assertion
options.description: Simpler fixture, but every test asserts through a filter you wrote rather than through RLS. A dropped or broken RLS policy would pass silently — the exact 'passes by never running' failure this repo already shipped twice.

questions.question: Three source-health defects share one root: the counters are lifetime and keyed per-VENDOR, not per-attempt. A per-attempt table costs ~107k rows/yr (~11 MB). Which grain? (psot-a03)

options.label: Append-only per-attempt table (Recommended)
options.description: source_health_attempts(tenant_id, vendor, company_id, ok, error_class, ts); derive rollups from it. Dissolves all three defects at once: no rollback loss, no sibling-success clobber, and success_rate_24h becomes genuinely windowable. Adds per-COMPANY grain, so you learn WHICH board went dark — which invariant #23 asks for and the vendor-keyed table cannot answer. ~11 MB/yr.

options.label: Keep the lifetime rollup, patch each defect
options.description: No migration. Fix the rollback, the clobber and the window as three separate patches. Smaller diff now, but the table stays vendor-keyed so it still can't say which of 236 greenhouse boards is failing.

questions.question: What maximum age of max(last_seen_at) per board counts as stale? This becomes the alert threshold AND the on-screen freshness claim. Note it's a last_seen_at guarantee, not published_at. (psot-c01)

options.label: 48h — tolerates one missed run (Recommended)
options.description: Flags 73 of 266 boards today (27%), which is honest — those are genuinely stale, including a cluster of 70 sitting at 63h. Absorbs exactly one skipped daily run before crying wolf. Suggested tenant target: 95% of boards inside SLA.

options.label: 24h — strictest
options.description: Flags 109 of 266 (41%) today. On a daily schedule every board is ~24h old just before the next run, so this alerts constantly and gets muted — the classic dead alarm.

options.label: 72h — loosest
options.description: Flags only 2 of 266 today. Tolerates two missed runs, but lets the 70 boards currently at 63h read as perfectly healthy, which is the blind spot we're trying to close.

questions.question: When is a posting_snapshots row written, and what retention? Append-only is non-negotiable either way (invariant #10). (psot-h04)

options.label: On change + periodic heartbeat (Recommended)
options.description: Write when payload_hash changes, plus one heartbeat row per posting per week so 'still open, unchanged' stays provable. Measured: only 15,873 distinct payload states exist across 21,175 rows — changes are rare, so this keeps the audit timeline meaningful at a fraction of the volume.

options.label: Every poll
options.description: Maximum fidelity: every observation recorded. ~5.8M rows and ~1.3 GB/yr for this one tenant, the overwhelming majority byte-identical to the row before.

options.label: On change only, no heartbeat
options.description: Leanest. But absence then means two different things — 'unchanged' and 'we never looked' — which is precisely the conflation the freshness work exists to remove.
